title: Skolem problem
formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine which, for every input consisting of an integer \(k\ge1\), integer coefficients \(c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1}\), and integer initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(u_t=0\) for some integer \(t\ge0\), where the infinite sequence is uniquely defined by \[u_{t+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}c_j u_{t+j}\qquad(t=0,1,2,\ldots)?\] The order \(k\) is part of the input and is unrestricted; no time or space bound is requested.
definitions: Use input alphabet \(\{0,1,+,-,\#\}\). For a nonnegative integer \(a\), let \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\) be its ordinary base-two expansion without leading zeros, with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Encode an integer \(z\) by a plus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(z)\) if \(z\ge0\), and by a minus sign followed by \(\operatorname{bin}(-z)\) if \(z<0\); negative zero is invalid. A valid input is \(\operatorname{bin}(k)\), then exactly \(k\) signed coefficient fields in order, then exactly \(k\) signed initial-value fields in order, separated by one \(\#\) between consecutive fields, with no other symbols or trailing separator. The first field has \(k\ge1\). Output 1 means that a zero occurs at some nonnegative index, including among the initial values; output 0 means that every term at a nonnegative index is nonzero. The machine must halt with one of these two outputs on every valid input and reject every malformed input with output 0. This decidable syntax convention does not affect the underlying decidability question. A deterministic Turing machine has one finite transition table, a finite alphabet and finitely many work tapes; it has no randomness, external oracle, advice or input-dependent program. The sequence values are exact integers with no bound on their magnitude, and the same fixed coefficients apply at every index. The listed recurrence need not have the smallest possible order. Coefficients and initial values may vanish, all may be zero, and \(c_0=0\) is allowed; forward evolution is still uniquely defined. In particular, neither distinct characteristic roots nor a non-degeneracy assumption is promised. No upper bound on the index of a possible zero is supplied. This is a discrete-time existence-of-a-zero question, with indices \(0,1,2,\ldots\); negative or real-valued indices and nonnegativity of all terms are different targets.

context_blocks.text: Every individual term of the sequence is effectively computable from the finite input, and the existence of a zero is semidecidable: positive instances have a finite witnessing index. The unresolved demand is a procedure guaranteed to finish on zero-free inputs too. The problem concerns the whole class of input sequences; undecidability would not mean that the zero question for each particular named recurrence is unanswerable.

The same recurrence describes linear dynamics in \(k\)-dimensional integer space. With \(v_t=(u_t,\ldots,u_{t+k-1})^{\mathsf T}\), let \(B\) have ones just above the diagonal, zeros in the other entries of its first \(k-1\) rows, and last row \((c_0,\ldots,c_{k-1})\). Then \(v_{t+1}=Bv_t\), including when \(k=1\). The question is whether this orbit reaches the hyperplane where the first coordinate is zero. This makes the connection to exact reachability and termination guards in linear programs explicit.

The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem says that the zero indices form a finite union of arithmetic progressions, together with a finite exceptional set. Here a progression has the form \(\{a+br:r\ge0\}\), with integers \(a\ge0\) and \(b\ge1\). That qualitative structure does not itself provide an effective description of all exceptional zeros. The distinction between a structural existence theorem and an algorithm extracting its finite data is central to this problem.

Many sources assume that the coefficient of the oldest term is nonzero, which permits extending the sequence backward. The card retains arbitrary forward recurrences. A zero oldest-term coefficient can contribute a finite initial prefix before a recurrence of smaller order with nonzero oldest-term coefficient; the all-zero-coefficient case is eventually zero. Thus this input convention does not replace the classical decision problem with a different restriction. Rational coefficients and initial values also lead to the same zero-decision problem as integer data by an effective nonzero scaling, as explained in the 2026 survey.

For the recurrences considered in the cited number-theoretic results, the characteristic polynomial is the polynomial of a minimal-order recurrence. A sequence is simple when its characteristic roots are distinct, and non-degenerate when the ratio of no two distinct roots is a root of unity; a root of unity is a complex number whose positive integer power is one. These are different restrictions. Neither is imposed by the card. For nonzero non-degenerate sequences the zero set is finite, but no general effective bound on all those zeros is known in the inspected sources.

Bilu and coauthors’ MFCS 2022 Theorem 3 gives decidability for simple recurrences assuming both the Exponential Local-Global Principle, also called the Skolem Conjecture, and the weak p-adic Schanuel Conjecture. Their procedure produces an unconditional correctness certificate whenever it terminates; the universal termination assertion is conditional. The similarly named Skolem Conjecture is an additional arithmetic hypothesis, not the decision problem on this card.

Bacik, Ouaknine and Worrell’s SODA 2026 work, with a corrected arXiv revision of 17 July, places the order-at-most-four problem in coRP. For this zero-existence language, coRP means a randomized polynomial-time test accepting zero-containing inputs with probability one and rejecting zero-free inputs with probability at least one half. They also give such a bound for the bounded-index problem at each fixed order, where the upper index is supplied in binary. The latter remains restricted by that supplied bound; fixed-order complexity statements do not decide arbitrary unbounded-order recurrences.

Luca, Ouaknine and Worrell’s July 2026 Theorem 4.3 yields general decidability conditional on their Conjecture 4.2, which extends a Cramér–Granville prime-gap hypothesis to a specially defined density-one subset of primes. Ordinary prime-gap conjectures are not silently substituted for that stronger assumption. The same paper proves unconditionally the existence of a recursive index set \(S\) of natural density one on which zero existence is decidable for every recurrence. Density one means \(|S\cap\{0,\ldots,N\}|/(N+1)\to1\). Missing indices can still contain a recurrence’s only zero, so this does not decide existence over all nonnegative indices.

The joint survey dated 26 July 2026 continues to list both general Skolem and Positivity as open. Positivity asks whether all terms are nonnegative, while Bi-Skolem allows negative as well as nonnegative integer indices in a backward-extendible sequence. Continuous Skolem instead concerns zeros at real times in a linear differential equation. Results in these settings, or over rings of positive characteristic, have different input or index domains and are not resolutions of this integer recurrence target.

why: Skolem asks whether exact reachability of zero is decidable for the simplest class of discrete linear recurrences with finite integer descriptions. The question connects arithmetic with verification of linear loops, matrix dynamics, automata and stochastic systems, and serves as a common unresolved decision problem to which other verification tasks are compared.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a total decision machine exists, with termination and correctness for every valid input and rejection of malformed strings, or a Lean-checked proof that no such machine exists. Equivalently, the language of valid encodings whose sequences contain a zero must be proved decidable or undecidable. A negative answer must rule out every total deterministic decider, not merely give an input on which one proposed program fails. A positive answer has to decide both the zero and zero-free cases uniformly over all orders; a semidecision procedure, a bounded-index algorithm, a theorem for a fixed order, or conditional termination under an unproved number-theoretic assumption does not settle the full target. A complexity lower bound such as NP-hardness does not prove undecidability. No polynomial bound, bound on the first zero, or enumeration of the entire zero set is required as the output.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability problem with an elementary finite input, substantial arithmetic content, and direct links to verification and automata. The 2026 work confirms current specialist attention; the importance is independent of the record’s previous incomplete wording.

progress.text: The Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem describes zero sets as finitely many arithmetic progressions plus a finite set; the inspected primary papers explain why this is not an effective solution of the decision problem.
The MFCS paper gives a procedure for simple recurrences with unconditional correctness certificates upon termination, but termination on every input depends on two number-theoretic conjectures.

The SODA low-order result places order at most four in coRP; the inspected third arXiv version of 17 July corrects Lemma 3.2. Its bounded-index result for each fixed order retains the index bound as input.
The general conditional decidability paper uses a strengthened Cramér–Granville hypothesis and separately gives an unconditional Universal Skolem Set of density one.
The new joint survey explicitly retains the unrestricted integer Skolem problem as open and separates Positivity, Bi-Skolem and other settings.

sentences: The Skolem problem asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide if any given integer linear recurrence ever has a zero term.
The input lists its order, coefficients and initial values in binary, with no restriction on order or repeated characteristic roots and no upper bound on the index.
Every single term can be computed, but a decision procedure must also finish when the infinite sequence has no zero.
The question is a basic exact reachability problem in linear dynamics with connections to program verification and automata.
A complete Lean proof must establish decidability or undecidability for all inputs; conditional termination, low-order algorithms and density-one index sets do not settle that target.
